claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a predominantly FCC matrix.
The starting alloy has a homogeneous FCC microstructure and well-controlled additive-manufacturing features.
Elevated-temperature degradation is governed by whether a protective oxide scale forms.
The governing protective scale is enriched in Al2O3 and TiO2.
Oxidizing conditions cause Al and Ti to migrate preferentially to the alloy surface.
Under oxidizing conditions, Al and Ti form a dense, continuous, and coherent oxide scale.
An Al2O3/TiO2-rich surface scale impedes further oxygen ingress.
Restricting oxygen ingress preserves the alloy microstructure and mechanical strength.
Reducing gas conditions suppress formation of the protective oxide scale because oxygen availability is limited.
Suppression or disruption of the protective scale causes more pervasive internal oxidation.
Cr, Fe, and Ni undergo internal oxidation under the proposed reducing conditions.
Internal oxidation under reducing conditions accelerates embrittlement and mechanical degradation.
Oxidizing exposure will minimize further oxidation and maintain mechanical integrity relative to the starting-state baseline.
Reducing exposure will produce a higher degradation rate and lower hardness and tensile strength than the baseline.
Oxidation kinetics and oxide phase assemblages in high-entropy alloys can vary substantially between 600 and 900 degrees Celsius.
Different oxidation kinetics or phase transformations may dominate outside the proposed 600–900 degrees Celsius boundary.
Processing-induced defects or local compositional variations may affect protective-scale nucleation and growth.
SEM and XRD can characterize oxide-scale morphology and phase composition after exposure.
A controlled comparison at 700 degrees Celsius for 100 hours between oxidizing and reducing atmospheres can distinguish the proposed scale-controlled mechanism.
Similar scale properties and statistically indistinguishable mechanical degradation in the two atmospheres would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The reducing atmosphere is said to suppress oxide formation because oxygen availability is limited, yet it is also predicted to cause more pervasive internal oxidation. No oxygen source, oxygen-potential window, or transport mechanism is provided to reconcile reduced external oxidation with increased internal oxidation.
